title: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye agree in principle on a joint military command
dek: At Islamabad talks, the three Makkah pact members condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and moved to give their alliance a civilian secretariat and a military headquarters, Türkiye's foreign minister said.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye have agreed in principle to give their three-month-old mutual-defence pact a joint military command as well as a civilian secretariat, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said after the alliance's top committee met in Islamabad on Friday. The joint statement issued after the talks did not mention a military command, and Mr Fidan said some details had been held over to the next meeting, which Türkiye will host.

The three governments also condemned what their statement called "persistent and heinous attacks by the Houthi militia" on civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, and pledged to step up support for the kingdom's security under the pact's collective-defence provisions. For India, the meeting is a sign that a bloc binding Pakistan's armed forces to two of the most influential states in the Muslim world is turning from a signed text into a working institution.

## What happened

The Strategic Political and Defence Committee, the alliance's highest decision-making body, met for about two and a half hours in Islamabad on Friday, 27 November, according to reports. It was the committee's second regular session, after an inaugural meeting in Istanbul on 31 August and an emergency session in Riyadh on 5 October.

Each country sent its foreign minister, defence minister and military chief. Pakistan was represented by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif and Field Marshal Asim Munir, the Chief of Defence Forces and Army Chief. Saudi Arabia sent Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Chief of General Staff General Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili. Türkiye sent Mr Fidan, Defence Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu.

According to the joint statement, as carried by Pakistan's state broadcaster, the committee reaffirmed the three countries' commitment to collective defence, mutual solidarity and respect for each other's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It reviewed progress on decisions taken in Istanbul and Riyadh, welcomed progress in setting up the alliance's secretariat in Saudi Arabia, and agreed to widen cooperation in defence industries, joint technology development, military training and capacity-building. It also agreed to keep up political and military consultations, to support de-escalation and to encourage the peaceful resolution of disputes.

Speaking afterwards, Mr Fidan said the members had agreed in principle on a Secretariat-General as the alliance's civilian headquarters and a Joint Military Command as its military arm, according to reports. He said most decisions had already been approved, that the alliance was institutionalising faster than comparable pacts, and that members had also agreed in principle on a roadmap and procedures for other countries that want to join. No candidate country was named and the principles were not published.

Mr Fidan said the committee had also discussed how negotiations between the United States and Iran could be steered towards a positive result, according to reports.

## Background

The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement was signed on 7 August by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. Its central clause treats an armed attack on any one of the three as an attack on all. It builds on the bilateral Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement that Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed in September 2025.

Help under the pact is not automatic: an attacked member must ask for it, and the three decide its nature and scope by consensus, according to earlier reporting on the text. New members need the unanimous consent of the founders, and members cannot withdraw for the first ten years. Türkiye's parliament ratified the agreement on 5 November by 279 votes to 119.

At the emergency meeting in Riyadh on 5 October, called after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the committee appointed a retired Pakistani officer, Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood, as the alliance's first secretary-general for a three-year term, according to Pakistan's Foreign Office. That meeting also discussed arrangements for the rapid deployment of agreed forces to Saudi Arabia, without disclosing their size, according to reports.

The Islamabad talks came as Saudi Arabia faces repeated missile and drone attacks from Yemen's Houthis on its cities, airports and oil facilities, and as the wider Gulf remains on edge over the US blockade of Iranian ports and this week's deadly drone strike in Kuwait.

## What they are saying

Mr Dar said the meeting reflected the three countries' determination to work for regional peace and stability, according to reports. Mr Asif said before the meeting that "any threat to Saudi Arabia is a threat to Pakistan and Türkiye according to the pact", and that Pakistan would use "whatever means are available" to defend the kingdom against Houthi attacks, according to reports. Asked how the alliance would respond to a direct Iranian attack on Saudi Arabia, he declined to say, and named Israel as a possible threat to countries in the region, one report said.

Pakistan describes the pact as defensive and says it is not directed against any country, including Iran. Saudi Arabia has said the arrangement is not a military alliance or religious bloc and has nothing to do with nuclear weapons, according to earlier reports. Mr Fidan has said the alliance is open to regional states that accept its principles, such as respect for sovereignty and non-interference.

India has not commented on the Islamabad meeting. When the pact was signed in August, the External Affairs Ministry's spokesperson, Randhir Jaiswal, said India was examining its implications for national security and regional stability and remained "fully committed" to safeguarding its national interest. After the 2025 Saudi-Pakistan agreement, he said India expected its strategic partnership with Riyadh to "keep in mind mutual interests and sensitivities".

## Why it matters for India

Saudi Arabia is one of India's largest suppliers of crude oil and home to one of the biggest Indian communities abroad, and New Delhi describes Riyadh as a strategic partner. Türkiye's president has repeatedly raised Kashmir at the UN General Assembly, drawing protests from New Delhi. A standing joint command would give Pakistan's military a formal, permanent role in the defence of the Gulf's largest economy, and a Pakistani officer already heads the alliance's secretariat.

The pact's terms matter for how far that goes. Because assistance must be requested and agreed by consensus, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye would not be automatically drawn into a conflict involving Pakistan. But the alliance's growing defence-industrial cooperation, joint training and possible expansion to other states will shape the security environment in the Arabian Sea and the Gulf, where India's energy imports pass and where millions of Indians live and work.

## What happens next

- Next committee meeting: to be hosted by Türkiye, date not announced. Deferred details of the joint command and secretariat are to be settled there, Mr Fidan said.
- Secretariat: being set up in Saudi Arabia under Lt Gen (retd) Nauman Mahmood.
- Membership: a roadmap for new members has been agreed in principle; no country has been named. Syria has said discussions on joining are under way, according to earlier reports.
- The agreement enters into force once all three countries have deposited their ratification documents with the secretariat.
